summary.text: Title and authors: "Lightweight Compositional Embeddings for Incremental Streaming Recommendation" by Mengyue Hang (Purdue University), Tobias Schnabel and Longqi Yang (Microsoft), and Jennifer Neville (Purdue University and Microsoft).

blocks.title: Abstract
blocks.content:
Most work in graph-based recommender systems considers a
static setting where all information about test nodes (i.e., users and
items) is available upfront at training time. However, this static
setting makes little sense for many real world applications where
data comes in continuously as a stream of new edges and nodes,
and one has to update model predictions incrementally to reflect
the latest state. To fully capitalize on the newly available data in the
stream, recent graph-based recommendation models would need to
be repeatedly retrained, which is infeasible in practice. In this pa-
per,

summary.text: Abstract. Graph-based recommenders usually assume a static setting where everything about test users and items is known at training time, but real data arrives as a stream of new edges and nodes, and retraining to keep up is impractical. The paper proposes Lightweight Compositional Embedding (LCE), which learns explicit embeddings for only one node type and represents the other implicitly, by composing over its graph interactions, so it can be updated incrementally at low cost when one type (such as items) suits a static representation. On three large user-item datasets in a streaming setting, the authors report that LCE beats competitive baselines and comes close to skyline performance with far fewer parameters than other graph-based models.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Real-world recommender systems face a number of important
challenges in practice. First, they need to be able to model the rich-
ness of user-item and user-user interactions. Graph-based recom-
mender systems are an excellent fit for this as they frame recommen-
dation as a link prediction task on the user-item graph [10, 32, 36].
Another substantial challenge is the dynamic nature of the inter-
action data that recommendations are based on. For example, on
most content platforms, users continuously interact with items (e.g.,
subscribe to a channel, visit a location) and with each other (e.g.,

summary.text: Introduction. Graph-based recommenders frame recommendation as link prediction on the user-item graph, but interaction data streams in continuously, while most work assumes a static setting, which hurts cold-start performance and forces regular retraining. The paper studies top-k recommendation under streaming data (long-term interests, as distinct from next-item sequential recommendation). LCE learns a static representation for the node type that is more amenable to one (for example, items) and a compositional function for the other, which lets it update without relearning, use fewer parameters than fully explicit models, and make partially inductive predictions for new nodes of the composed type. The contributions are a formalisation of incremental streaming graph recommendation, the LCE method, and results under an incremental replay protocol, including cold-start items and a Microsoft Teams production setting.

3.1
LCE model
We start with a general description of the LCE model before
turning to training and inference details. For ease of exposition, let
us assume that we chose to learn explicit embeddings for 𝑢∈𝑈
and represent 𝑤∈𝑊implicitly through a composition function.
LCE then represents each user 𝑢via a pair of explicit embeddings
(z𝑢, ˜z𝑢

summary.text: The LCE model. Taking users as the explicitly embedded type, each user u has two embeddings (z_u, z̃_u), one for aggregation and one for scoring, and the edge probability is S(u, w) = σ(z̃_uᵀ z_w); recommendations rank items by this score. An item's initial embedding composes the embeddings of the users it interacted with, by mean or sum pooling (Eq. 2), and L graph-convolution layers then propagate information through the graph, with the final item embedding the average of all layers (Eqs. 3 and 4). Following LightGCN, aggregation is mean pooling and the layer transformation is the identity. In offline training the explicit embeddings are fitted with simplified GCN layers; in each update the compositional embeddings and scores are recomputed with the new edges.

summary.text: Replay protocol, data and baselines. Data is split by time into an offline training set with validation, K streaming chunks, and a test set; models are trained once offline, then fed each streaming chunk with parameters fixed, and compared with skyline models retrained on all data so far, using recall@N and nDCG@N on the new test edges. The datasets are Yelp (20,458 users, 37,552 items), Epinions (10,277 users, 87,791 items, with a trust network) and LibraryThing (16,894 users, 59,079 items, with social links), with their time windows in Table 1; since items outnumber users, users are embedded explicitly and items compositionally. Baselines (Table 2) are Top-Popu, ALS, ENSFM, RP3β, SLIM and LightGCN, plus two LCE ablations; ENSFM, which cannot update incrementally, is retrained instead.

summary.text: Comparison with baselines. In Table 3 (recall@20 and nDCG@20 after the last streaming chunk), almost every method improves with streaming data, the exception being LightGCN on Yelp, and LCE beats all baselines, by 5.2% to 17.1% over the best one, significantly so in the starred cells by paired t-test. LightGCN and SLIM are the strongest baselines; LCE beats LightGCN while having fewer parameters whenever the composed node set is the larger. In Figure 2, LCE's gap between incremental updates and skyline retraining is the smallest of the methods compared, and each incremental step takes seconds against hours to retrain. With cold-start items on Epinions and LibraryThing (Figure 3), LCE improves on SLIM and ALS, the baselines that can handle new items.

Using one user embedding instead of two (LCE-1 emb) is slightly worse than full LCE but still comparable to or better than LightGCN, and a single GCN layer (LCE-1 layer) is worse than three, supporting the value of separate aggregation and scoring embeddings and of multiple layers. Mean and sum composition give comparable results. Figures 2 and 3, and Table 4 and Figure 4 of the next section, are placed in this block.

blocks.title: Explicit v.s. implicit embeddings
blocks.content:
One important assumption of our model is that one node type
is more amenable to “static” representation than the other, so we
learn a static representation for that node type (e.g, users) and learn
an implicit, compositional function to calculate the representation
of the other nodes (e.g, items). In our earlier experiments, we con-
sidered the smaller node set to be the more static one, which is
the set of users in all the three datasets. We also tried the reverse
(i.e. explicitly embedding items and using a compositional func-
tion for users). Let the embedding dimension of LCE-item be 𝑑𝑖�

summary.text: Explicit against implicit embeddings. Reversing the design, embedding items explicitly and composing users, performs significantly worse, whether the parameter count is held equal or doubled (Table 4). To test the stationarity assumption, the authors split training data into four chronological buckets, learn LightGCN embeddings on the first, then fix one node type and relearn the other on later buckets: fixing users and updating items does consistently better (Figure 4), which they read as items being the more non-stationary type in these datasets, and as support for composing the non-stationary type.

blocks.title: Evaluation on real-world production data
blocks.content:
In additional to the three public datasets, we also evaluated
LCE on a real-world production system (Microsoft Teams), where
the task is to recommend TEAMs for users to join. We created a
subset of 224K users and 26K TEAMs, with a total of 65 million user
interactions. The interaction graph is constructed from a set of time-
stamped user-item and user-user actions, where the edges represent
interactions between two users (accessing a shared document, email
communication, chatting), or between a user and a TEAM (past
membership). The offline, streaming and test time windows are set
to 3 weeks,

summary.text: Evaluation on production data from Microsoft Teams, recommending teams for users to join: 224K users, 26K teams and 65 million interactions, with offline, streaming and test windows of 3 weeks, 2 weeks and 5 months and daily streaming slices. Against LightGCN, LCE matched offline performance with over 80% fewer parameters and was up to 6.42% better on precision@3 with streaming data; LCE kept improving with more streaming data while LightGCN did not, possibly, the authors suggest, because of over-parameterisation.

Sequential and streaming recommendation
Sequential recommendation models [5, 16, 20, 21, 29, 33, 35] fo-
cus on capturing the temporal dynamics of user-item interactions

tion. Moreover, these methods cannot handle non-bipartite graph
data which we study in this paper. Regarding streaming recommen-
dation, prior work [3, 7, 31] has proposed retraining models with
subsamples of the training set [31] or meta-learning [37]. However,
so far, these techniques are only shown to be effective for shallow
MF models that do not capture hig

summary.text: Related work on sequential and streaming recommendation (the block's heading is misplaced by the extraction). Sequential recommenders model the temporal dynamics of interactions, which the authors call orthogonal to incremental recommendation, and cannot handle non-bipartite graphs. Prior streaming recommenders retrain on subsamples or use meta-learning, but have only been shown to work for shallow matrix-factorisation models, and retraining is not practical for large deep or graph-based models; LCE is presented as a graph-based model that supports incremental recommendation.

blocks.title: Graph-based recommendation models
blocks.content:
Leveraging graphs to support recommendation scenarios is an
emerging research theme. The core idea is to cast recommenda-
tion problem to graph link prediction. Prior work explored many
graph neural network architectures, for example GraphSage [9, 36].
NGCF [32] and LightGCN [10] learn convolutional structures over
embeddings for all users and items. These models are not generally
applicable to the incremental streaming recommendation setting
that this paper studied, because they require either auxiliary fea-
tures [9, 36] or explicit embeddings for all nodes [10, 32]. Our work
follows the lin

summary.text: Related work on graph-based and cold-start recommendation. Graph recommenders such as GraphSage-based models, NGCF and LightGCN cast recommendation as link prediction but need auxiliary features or explicit embeddings for every node, so they do not fit the incremental streaming setting, which LCE's compositional embeddings do. Some non-graph models also represent users by the items they interacted with to address cold start, but cold start assumes a static setting; LCE handles new entities of its composed type and improves over matrix factorisation and SLIM on cold-start items. A fully inductive version could compose over stationary objects or node attributes.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
Motivated by needs of real-world recommender systems, we
consider recommendation in an incremental streaming setting in
this work, where new data continuously comes in after the model
is trained. This is in contrast to the static setting that most graph-
based recommendation systems adopt where all information about
test nodes are available at training time. We propose a composi-
tional graph-based method (LCE) that supports continuous updates
in a streaming setting under low computational cost. To evaluate
the proposed method, we conduct experiments on three real-world

summary.text: Conclusion. The paper considers recommendation in an incremental streaming setting, where data keeps arriving after training, and proposes LCE, a compositional graph-based method that supports cheap continuous updates. On three real-world datasets it outperforms competitive baselines, uses streaming data effectively, in many cases approaching skyline performance as if retrained on all data, and improves markedly on cold-start items; results in a Microsoft Teams production setting were also positive.

The references cover graph and factorisation recommenders (LightGCN, NGCF, PinSage, SLIM, ALS, ENSFM, RP3β), sequential, dynamic and streaming recommendation, cold-start methods, and the datasets. The appendix compares LCE with related methods (Table 5, where LCE is the only one marked as supporting new items, efficient incremental updates, top-k prediction and user-user links without needing features), gives training details (Xavier initialisation, Adam, up to 800 epochs with early stopping on validation recall@20, three GCN layers), dataset filtering, and baseline settings. Table 6 gives offline results, where LCE's margins over the best baseline range from −0.69% (Yelp recall) to +17.07%. On model capacity, LCE learns 2|U|d parameters against LightGCN's (|U| + |W|)d, about five times fewer on Epinions, and Figure 5 shows LCE competitive offline and clearly better with streaming data at a much smaller size.
